analysis.one_liner: Replaces drug patents with government prizes, letting anyone sell copies of approved medicines.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by a single independent lawmaker with no cosponsors, sat in two House committees for two years and never received a hearing or a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have ended the patent monopolies and exclusive marketing periods that let brand-name drug companies be the only sellers of a medicine in the U.S. Instead, anyone who met FDA standards could make and sell any approved drug, and the companies that invented the drugs would be rewarded from a new federal prize fund, sized at 0.5 percent of the entire economy each year. A 13-member board would decide who got prizes and how much, based on how many patients a drug helped, how much better it was than existing treatments, and whether it addressed neglected diseases that mainly afflict the world's poor.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and consumers, who could buy any approved medicine from any manufacturer, the way generic competition drives prices toward the cost of production. Generic and smaller drug makers would gain the right to make any approved drug on day one. Guaranteed shares of the fund (at least 4 percent for global neglected diseases, 10 percent for orphan drugs, and 4 percent for global infectious diseases including AIDS and bioterrorism medicines) would steer money toward diseases that monopoly markets ignore. Insurers, employers, and government programs that buy drugs would pay less.

how_it_helps.text: After October 1, 2007, no one would have exclusive rights to manufacture, distribute, sell, or use a drug, biological product, or manufacturing process, overriding patent rights and exclusive marketing periods such as Hatch-Waxman exclusivities, pediatric extensions, and orphan drug marketing exclusivity.

The bill's findings note that prescription drug spending hit $179.2 billion in 2003, prices rose 7.4 percent a year from 1993 to 2003 (nearly triple inflation), and consumers paid 30 percent of drug costs out of pocket — $53.2 billion.

The prize fund would reward inventors in place of monopoly sales, with prizes based on the number of patients helped (including patients abroad), the incremental therapeutic benefit over existing drugs, priority needs like neglected diseases, and improved manufacturing efficiency.

At least 4 percent of the fund would go to global neglected diseases, 10 percent to orphan drugs, and 4 percent to global infectious diseases and other priorities including AIDS research and bioterrorism medicines.

The board's criteria-setting and award decisions would be subject to open-records and open-meeting laws and a description of its methods and data that lets the public understand how decisions were reached, and the Government Accountability Office would audit the board every year.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers, through a mandatory federal appropriation each year equal to 0.5 percent of gross domestic product — roughly $60 billion annually at mid-2000s economy size. Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers would lose the monopoly rents that come from being the sole seller of patented drugs. Generic makers would still sell in a competitive market, so they would earn less per pill than a monopolist.

drawbacks.text: The fund would be a permanent federal appropriation of 0.5 percent of GDP each year regardless of how many drugs were developed or how much patients actually saved — a very large fixed commitment, on the order of $60 billion a year at the time, taken on before anyone knew whether the prize board would judge innovation well.

Rewards would be set by a 13-member government board (four agency heads and nine presidential appointees) using criteria it writes itself, capped at 5 percent of the annual fund for any single drug and 10 years of payments. If the board undervalued a breakthrough, the inventor would have no monopoly revenues to fall back on; if it overvalued a minor drug, taxpayers would overpay.

The bill was never amended, costed, or tested in a hearing, so its transition arbitration scheme for drugs already under multiple patents and its treatment of existing products were never refined through the committee process.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: cheap copies of every approved medicine in exchange for a large, permanent federal prize fund that replaces patent-based pricing. Patients would almost certainly pay far less at the pharmacy, and research money would flow to neglected diseases that markets neglect. But the design puts an enormous amount of discretion in a new government board, commits a fixed share of the whole economy every year, and was never examined in a hearing or scored, so its actual costs and its effect on long-run drug innovation were untested. A more gradual or pilot version might have been worth trying; as introduced, it asked Congress to accept a lot of uncertainty at once.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and their subcommittees in early 2005, and neither committee ever held a hearing or sent it anywhere, so it died quietly when the Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Representative Bernard Sanders, an Independent from Vermont, introduced the bill on January 26, 2005.
No other member of the House joined as a cosponsor at any point in the two-year Congress.

The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Judiciary Committee on the day of introduction, then in February 2005 to the Health Subcommittee and the Courts, the Internet, and Intellectual Property Subcommittee.
The congressional record shows no further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — after those referrals.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, who kept their patent-based exclusive marketing rights and the monopoly prices that come with them, and patients continued to pay among the highest drug prices in the world. The members of Congress who declined to take up a politically difficult idea also avoided the fight.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand-name drug makers kept their monopolies

for.name: Bernard Sanders
for.what_they_did: Sponsored and introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on it; no other member cosponsored it.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of primary referral (Chair Joe Barton, R-TX)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral, sent it to its Health Subcommittee, and never held a hearing or markup on it in two years.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of additional referral (Chair F. James Sensenbrenner, R-WI)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral, sent it to its Courts, the Internet, and Intellectual Property Subcommittee, and never took it up.

against.name: Brand-name pharmaceutical industry
against.role: Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America and its member companies
against.what_they_did: The industry publicly opposed replacing patent-based drug pricing with a government prize fund, the core of the bill.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a point where party lines could form: its only sponsor was an Independent, and no member of either party ever cosigned it.

industries.note: The bill would end the exclusive rights — patents, Hatch-Waxman and orphan drug exclusivity, pediatric extensions — that let these companies be the sole seller of a medicine and charge monopoly prices. Their existing revenue model is exactly what the bill replaces.

Once exclusivity ended, any manufacturer meeting FDA standards could make and sell every approved drug immediately, giving them a vastly larger addressable market. Their competitive pricing is the mechanism that would lower patients' costs.

The bill would guarantee minimum shares of the prize fund — 4 percent for global neglected diseases, 10 percent for orphan drugs, 4 percent for global infectious diseases including AIDS and bioterrorism countermeasures — for diseases that monopoly pricing does not serve because patients cannot pay.

The fund would be a mandatory annual appropriation of 0.5 percent of GDP, several tens of billions of dollars a year, replacing consumer drug spending with federal spending. Whether taxpayers netted out ahead would depend on the prize board's judgment.
